blocks.text: Chulin 62a it is said: תורין של רחבה (turtledoves of the Rehaba) may be taken as an offering in place of the תורין, but not in place of the בני יונה; accordingly, with respect to size they stand between the young, small pigeon and the full-grown one. Ibid. 62b the תורין של רחבה are identified with the כפשני צוציני, and this latter name could help to determine the kind of dove. כפשני, for which Aruch reads כבשני, is the Aramaic translation of תורים, while the word צוציני is explained in various ways. Raschi and Buxdorf (Lex. pag. 1898) take it for a place name, which only makes the identification more difficult; Aruch (s.v. צץ), on the other hand, gives the following explanation: למה קורין איתן צוציני? שיש להן ציצית בראשיהן כמו שכתוב ויקחני בציצית ראשי, “Why are they called צוציני? Because they have locks on their heads, as it is said (Ezech. 8, 3): He took me by the locks of my head”; in this biblical passage the locks are called ציצית.

I suspect that the hooded pigeon (Columba livia cocullata) is meant here. The feathers of the back of the head and of the upper neck appear curved backwards and are directed upwards. They form a kind of monk's hood (Voigt l. c. 2. p. 331); cf. on ציצין §. 298.

Chulin 62a it is said that the dove חסיל may not be taken as an offering in place of the חורין, but may well be in place of the בני יונה; accordingly חסיל must be a very small dove. Here Raschi says: חסיל is a kind of dove, whereas on Chulin 140b: חסיל is a bird resembling the dove and is clean.

However, it is clear from the Chaldean paraphrase that חסיל served to designate young and small doves. Jonathan translates גמל (Gen. 15, 9) by: חסילא בר יון, likewise גוזליו (Deut 32, 11) by חסילוי; thus חסיל designates on the one hand the young dove, on the other hand the young of birds in general, and so Raschi's differing explanations become understandable. I suspect the very small tumbler pigeon (Columba livia gyratrix), which because of its smallness could be taken for בני יונה.
Landau translates: pouter pigeon; but precisely this pigeon is very large, since it inflates its crop enormously and in itself already has a very large crop (Blumenbach: Handb. der Naturg. p. 199).

The חסיל sometimes hatches eggs reciprocally with other doves (Chulin 140b), and when drinking sips the water in such a way that it lets it flow out again (מוצץ ומקיא, ibid. 62b). Noteworthy is Samuel's explanation (Rabba batra 75a) of ציצלא by חאציל; the latter word seems to stand, corrupted, for חסיל, and ציצלא designates, according to all the commentaries, a small bird; cf. §. 252.

We have already earlier (§. 233) mentioned a wild dove which takes its name from its colour and which lives in holes in trees; here we treat the wild dove which lives in clefts. For it is said in Gittin 69b that the dung of the חמימתא was used as a remedy for pains in the rectum. Raschi gives two explanations of the word. He himself explains it as dove, his teacher*), on the other hand, as hen. Raschi's explanation is the correct one, since the dove is also called حَمَامَةٌ [ḥamāma] in Arabic. [p. 206] Shaw (see Rosenmüller loc. cit. vol. 4, Part 2, p. 332) mentions a town in Africa named Hamamat, so called after the wild doves, since these nest in the clefts of the region there.

Probably the wild dove is also meant in the passage cited above (p. 202), according to which King Janai had a great number of young doves brought down from a tree, since it arrives in large flocks and also nests in trees. According to some, צפור דרור is also supposed to be the wild dove; cf. the following article.

The צפור דרור, “bird of freedom,” which is biblical and also occurs frequently in the Talmud, is explained in three ways. Landau takes it for the bird Dururi, an Egyptian bird of which Forskal (Descript. anim. p. 10) reports that toward the end of October it comes from Upper Egypt to Alexandria. However, apart from the fact that, as Winer (B. R. Wb. 2, p. 435) rightly remarks, we know nothing certain about this bird and the Arabic spelling of its name, the צפור דרור also appears in the Talmud as a bird present everywhere and not confined to a particular region. Others, such as the Chaldean (on Ps. 84, 3), Bochart (Hieroz. P. 2, lib. 1, cap. 8, col. 51 ff.) and Rosenmüller (loc. cit. 4, 2, p. 337), explain the צפור דרור as a kind of wild dove; the former translates it by שבנינא, and the latter two refer to the Arabic سَاقْ حُرٍّ [sāq ḥurr] (dove of freedom), so that the latter word حُرٍّ [ḥurr] corresponds to the Hebrew דרור, by which in particular the male of the wild dove is designated. But this bird too cannot be meant by the talmudic צפור דרור, for reasons still to be mentioned. We give here all the Talmud passages from which it emerges that צפור דרור designates the swallow.

Sota 16b it is said that the leper took the צפור דרור for the birds of his purification offering; if one compares with this the passage in Chulin 62a, where it says: “A bird that scratches with its feet (see the following article) may be taken for the purification offering of the leper, and this bird [p. 207] is the סנינית לבנה (white swallow),” then סנונית*) and צפור דרור are identical, which Raschi on the latter passage evidently indicates; he says: The צפור mentioned in the Bible in connection with that purification offering is the סנונית לבנה.
